analysis.one_liner: Stops health plans from capping mental health care more tightly than physical health care.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee without a vote; real parity for mental health coverage did not arrive until 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill told employers and insurers who offer mental health coverage that they could not set lower limits on mental health hospital stays or therapy visits than they set for physical illness. For severe illnesses like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression, insurers could not impose any special limits at all. It did not force any employer to offer mental health coverage, and it exempted companies with 25 or fewer employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families whose employer health plans cap mental health care more tightly than physical care. A person with major depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia who runs out of covered hospital days or therapy visits would keep getting insurance-covered treatment instead of paying out of pocket, going without care, or facing relapse and hospitalization.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with mental illness and their families

how_it_helps.text: Plans offering mental health benefits could no longer set a lower cap on mental health hospital days or outpatient visits than they set for medical and surgical care.

For severe biologically based illnesses—schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, PTSD, autism, anorexia, and ADHD—plans could not impose any limits at all unless the same limits applied to physical illness care.
The bill preserved stronger state parity laws, so states could keep or add protections beyond the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and insurers offering mental health benefits, who would absorb higher claims from expanded mental health coverage; small employers (25 or fewer workers) were exempted, concentrating the cost on larger plans.

drawbacks.text: Plans were not required to offer mental health benefits at all—parity rules only applied to plans that already offered them, so employers could drop the benefit rather than equalize it.
Employers with 25 or fewer employees were exempt, leaving workers at small businesses without these protections.
The bill regulated only hospital-day and outpatient-visit limits, not higher copayments or deductibles for mental health care, so insurers could still make mental health treatment costlier.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending separate, lower caps on mental health treatment for millions of insured workers—was substantial and the cost to employers and insurers modest compared with the gains to people whose care ran out mid-illness. The narrow carve-out for small employers (25 or fewer workers) and the refusal to mandate mental health benefits at all tempered it, but the design was sound and became the template for the 2008 federal parity law.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee held a hearing but never voted on the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor or the House.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 14, 1999 by Senator Domenici with six other original cosponsors and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee's only action was a hearing on May 18, 2000; no markup or vote was ever held.
With the 106th Congress ending January 3, 2001, the bill expired without reaching the Senate floor.
Its 28 cosponsors—21 Democrats and 7 Republicans—showed substantial cross-party support that never converted into floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers kept the ability to cap mental health coverage more tightly than medical coverage; patients who hit those caps kept paying out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers kept the caps

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone, Sen. Edward Kennedy, and other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors alongside Domenici, Chafee, Specter, Reid, and Sarbanes.

for.name: 28 senators (21 Democrats, 7 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on May 18, 2000, but never voted on it.

against.name: Employer coalitions and health insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanded mental health parity mandates as a costly requirement on employer health plans.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan and lopsided in breadth: all 28 cosponsors backing a Republican lead sponsor included 21 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but no vote ever tested the split.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill barred plans from using lower day and visit caps for mental health care, one of their main cost-control levers. It still allowed them to charge higher copays for mental health and to drop the benefit entirely, which limited the burden.
Psychiatrists, therapists, and psychiatric hospitals would see insurance cover more hospital days and outpatient visits, expanding paid treatment for the conditions the bill covered.
